1:
The alphabet is broken here, and the two who notice differ. Adam Clarke counts the damage: two letters are missing, one stands twice where a missing one should have been, and a whole line hangs at the end outside the series. He turns this into an indictment: it is fashionable, he says, to be violent in praise of the Jews for the faithfulness with which they preserved the Hebrew Scriptures, and such praise is in general ill placed, this psalm being proof of the carelessness with which the deposit was watched. He then repairs it from four manuscripts and six versions that keep the letter. Keil and Delitzsch take the same absence as original. They class it among nine alphabetical psalms and pair it with a companion that lacks the same letter, is parallel to it in sound and sense at three strophes, and likewise adds an extra strophe after the alphabet has run out; this homogeneousness, they say, points to one common author. What Clarke reads as neglect they read as a signature.

They differ over the occasion as flatly. Clarke refers the psalm to the captives in Babylon, and glosses those who deal treacherously as idolaters, putting a complaint against the Chaldeans into the speaker’s mouth. Keil and Delitzsch find no definite background indicating the history of the times and no clearly marked individuality at all, and read it instead as answering a question the preceding psalm had thrown out. Augustine of Hippo hears Christ speaking, but in the person of the Church, so that what is said belongs to the Christian people turned to God; he makes the shame of the second verse that of one who on abandoning God wished to be as God and then feared death from the smallest insect. John Calvin takes it for meditations mingled with prayers, in which David owns that God has justly used his enemies to chastise him.

The opening verb draws three readings, one of which Calvin rules out. John Gill offers lifting the soul in prayer on the authority of the Chaldee, as an offering like a living sacrifice, or as a deposit committed to God for keeping. Calvin names the second and rejects it: those who imagine David declares he had offered himself in sacrifice do not properly understand the passage, the meaning being that he does not gaze about for help from the world as the ungodly do. Matthew Henry makes prayer the ascent of the soul to God, and recalls the ancient call, Up with your hearts; C.H. Spurgeon allows that the soul often cannot rise, being more like a burrowing mole than a soaring eagle, and makes faith the lever and grace the arm until the loadstone of the Saviour’s love does the lifting.

Charles Ellicott corrects the English twice. Waiting on God should be waiting for him, the root meaning to make strong by twisting, and the received version errs in following an imperative found in the Greek, since the line is a promise that none who wait for God shall be ashamed, not a wish. Being led in truth he renders as being made to walk in it, an actual experience of divine faithfulness. Clarke separates the two words of the sixth verse, one the commiseration felt in the bowels at the sight of distress, the other kindnesses born of a profusion of benevolence. Keil and Delitzsch add that the will of God lies before us in the written word but that the expounder required to understand it is God himself, and close by quoting Augustine’s own prayer that God remember him not according to the anger he deserves but according to the mercy worthy of God. Gill refuses to let the sins of youth pass as follies of inadvertence, reading the plea as a confession of sinning from youth upward; John Wesley glosses being ashamed as being disappointed of hope.
8:
The petition for pardon sits in the middle of a run of promises, and Matthew Henry notices that it comes in abruptly and should have followed the seventh verse. What surprises him is the reason given: pardon it because it is great, the greater it is the more will mercy be magnified in forgiving it — when we confess sin we must aggravate it. C.H. Spurgeon argues the same way and calls it the logic of faith, clean contrary to that of a legal spirit, since pardoning a great sinner brings a great God great glory. John Wesley will not have it: the particle is often rendered though, so that the sense is pardon it although it is great, and the word means much as well as great, making the plea one of number rather than weight. Adam Clarke adds that there is no reason why God should show mercy but what he draws from the goodness of his own nature; John Gill and Wesley both suspect Bathsheba behind it.

On the teaching of the meek Keil and Delitzsch observe that one Hebrew word carries both the gentle and the humble, that Jerome renders it by the two words alternately in one verse, and that the poet repeats the one with lowliness uppermost; upon the self-righteous God would have to force himself against their will, whereas he wants disciples eager to learn. Clarke and Gill both press the word toward affliction, Clarke making them the poor and distressed whose cause God brings to a happy issue, Gill the miserable led on gently and by degrees as they can bear it.

Clarke digs into the paths: the word signifies the ruts wagon wheels make in ground crossed again and again, so that wherever we go mercy and truth can be seen to have passed by the depth of the tracks. Henry takes the paths for the promises and providences together, and finds it a rich satisfaction that this is how they will appear at the journey’s end. Charles Ellicott would render the pair grace and truth, and hears the conception of God passing from the domain of the Law to that of the Gospel.

The way that he shall choose divides them, and the versions are on the losing side. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the clause might be referred to God, the way in which he takes delight, as the Greek has it, but prefer on the strength of parallels the way the man should choose. Ellicott gives the same rendering while recording that the Greek and the Latin refer it to God. Wesley follows the versions and glosses it as the way God appoints; Henry declines to decide, since one who fears the Lord chooses what pleases him. Spurgeon turns it into a maxim: God does not violate our will but instructs it, and if we make our will his will he will let us have our will.

Four of them prefer the margin at the next verse, the soul lodging in goodness rather than dwelling at ease, Clarke saying the marginal reading is preferable, Keil and Delitzsch taking the verb of tarrying the night, Ellicott allowing the lodging and adding a sense of permanency. At the last verse Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott reach the same etymology independently: a sitting close together for confidential converse, and then the confidence itself. Ellicott derives it from a couch and the talk of those on it, offers the English word board as an analogy, and notes a borrowed word that travelled the same road backwards; Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek took it for strength, as though from another root. Clarke reads it as a secret assembly, many who fear God having a church in their house; Gill makes it the secret of the divine purposes; Wesley a favour known only to the one who enjoys it.
15:
The broken alphabet comes to a head at the eighteenth verse, and the two who disagreed about it at the opening disagree again. Adam Clarke observes that this is the verse which should begin with the missing letter, and that the following letter stands twice, here where it does not belong and in the next verse where it does; he reports two conjectural restorations, and concedes that the lost word has been gone so long that every version seems to have read what now stands in the Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch answer that the falling away of the letter is made up for by a doubled strophe of the other, and note that even the Greek has the imperative see twice over. Where Clarke sees a hole to be filled, they see a compensation already made.

Yet Keil and Delitzsch will emend the verse before it. The received division of the words, they say, gives only a poor antithesis and is to be suspected; the original text undoubtedly divided them otherwise, so that the line asks God to enlarge the straits of the heart and bring the man out of his distresses. Charles Ellicott reports the consensus of commentators for the same redivision and renders it as a plea that the sore heart be relieved and the sufferer released. John Gill keeps the received words but offers a second sense from them, that troubles have enlarged the heart, made a man wiser and increased his knowledge and experience, before deciding for the first. So the men who refused to touch the acrostic are the readiest to redivide a line, and the man who wanted the acrostic mended leaves this line as he found it.

On the desolation Keil and Delitzsch fix the word as meaning the only one of his kind, one who has no companion, and remark that the psalm does not avoid the chime of two words that sound alike, men treating him as a stranger so that God alone is left to complain to. Matthew Henry makes the loneliness deliberate: David calls himself desolate and solitary because he depended not upon his servants and soldiers but relied as entirely upon God as if he had no prospect of help from any creature. C.H. Spurgeon adds that unbelief suggests God has turned his back, that the ground of quarrel is always in ourselves, that saints never get beyond the publican’s prayer, and that one who trod the winepress alone can succour those on the solitary path. Clarke keeps his thesis that this is the prayer of the captives in Babylon, adding that the evils of a captive state, instead of lessening, seem to multiply.

Henry notices what the psalmist asks and what he does not. For his affliction he asks no more than that God look upon it and do as he pleases; for his sin he asks no less than full pardon, since in trouble we should be more concerned to have our sins pardoned than our afflictions removed. Keil and Delitzsch find it pleasing to a New Testament conscience that no vengeance is invoked upon the enemies, and define the hatred complained of as one that springs from injustice and ends in it. Gill supplies the history, the affliction being the rebellion of his subjects under his son and the pain the uneasiness of mind, or the fatigue of a man flying from place to place. On the eyes fixed upward Keil and Delitzsch make the constant look a praying mood that cannot go unanswered, and the net one of complicated circumstances he was ensnared in through no fault of his own; Henry contrasts it with idolaters, who were for gods they could see with their bodily eyes, whereas the eye turned toward a God who is a Spirit must be an eye of faith; John Wesley reduces the plucking to deliverance out of all troubles.
19:
Three of them agree that the psalm ends with a verse that was not originally part of it, and two of them give the same reason. Charles Ellicott says the closing line, which begins with a letter after the alphabet has run out, was apparently a later addition: not only is it an isolated line interfering with the alphabetical arrangement, but it differs from the rest of the psalm in the name it uses for God. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict independently, finding the connection with what precedes uncommonly loose and judging that the line looks added only when the psalm came into public worship, the change in the divine name favouring that view. Adam Clarke agrees that the verse stands out of the order of the psalm and does not appear to have formed part of the alphabetical arrangement, and takes it for a general prayer for redemption from captivity. Keil and Delitzsch push further: the companion alphabetical psalm closes with a supernumerary strophe under the same letter, and they wonder whether the two extra letters answer to two Greek letters of similar sound, or whether both show a habit of giving the final letters a special representation, as is sometimes done at the close of synagogue hymns.

What the closing prayer is for divides them less. John Gill takes it of a nation caught in the rebellion of a king’s son, and beyond that of the redemption of the spiritual Israel by the Messiah, from the law, from a stronger enemy, and from death itself. Clarke notices that the people had been prayed for through the preceding verses as if they were one person, and that the psalmist now takes in the whole lest his own necessities should narrow his heart and make him forget his fellow sufferers. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a principle, that the enmity of the world and of sin brings all who belong to God into the same straits, and that the need of the individual will not cease until the need of the whole has a radical remedy. John Wesley gives it the sharpest turn of all: if thou wilt not help me, yet spare thy people, who suffer for my sake and in my sufferings.

Gill will not settle whose integrity is meant in the verse before. It may be the psalmist’s own, pleaded as innocence in a government against which his subjects rebelled without cause; or it may be a prayer that those qualities remain with him, so that neither the corruptions of his heart nor the provocations of rebels drive him to act out of character; or it may be the integrity and uprightness of God, which is to say his goodness and his faithfulness to the covenant. Clarke reduces it to a wish for a perfect heart and an upright life. Keil and Delitzsch personify: devoutness that fills the whole man and uprightness that keeps to God’s will without bypaths are two guardians he asks for on a road made dangerous not only by outward enemies but by his own sinfulness, and these custodians are not to let him out of their sight.

On the enemies Gill asks for a look of another kind altogether, such as God gave the Egyptians through the pillar of fire, and observes that the arguments used are drawn from both the number of the enemies and their nature. Clarke reads the same plea as a confession of helplessness: God has only to look to see how impossible it is that the man should resist them. Keil and Delitzsch ground the prayer against disappointment in the fact that the hope rests in God himself, so that one who has taken refuge in him cannot be forsaken. Clarke notes that the psalm ends where it began, with the same plea against being put to shame.
